primaryText.he: וַיְדַבֵּר יְהֹוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה לֵּאמֹר. צַו אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וִישַׁלְּחוּ מִן הַמַּחֲנֶה כׇּל צָרוּעַ וְכׇל זָב וְכֹל טָמֵא לָנָפֶשׁ. מִזָּכָר עַד נְקֵבָה תְּשַׁלֵּחוּ אֶל מִחוּץ לַמַּחֲנֶה תְּשַׁלְּחוּם וְלֹא יְטַמְּאוּ אֶת מַחֲנֵיהֶם אֲשֶׁר אֲנִי שֹׁכֵן בְּתוֹכָם.
primaryText.en: The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Instruct the Israelites to remove from camp anyone with an eruption or a discharge and anyone defiled by a corpse. Remove male and female alike; put them outside the camp so that they do not defile the camp of those in whose midst I dwell.

text.en: Parshat Nasso is the longest parsha in the Torah.
It runs from the census of the Levites through the offerings of the tribal princes — laws, ordeals, blessings, gifts.
The opening command sets its central concern: who can stay in the camp where God dwells?
Send away anyone with an eruption, anyone with a discharge, anyone defiled by a corpse.
Lest they defile the camp of those in whose midst I dwell.
Nechama Leibowitz returned to this parsha twenty-eight times between 1942 and 1971.
Her gilyonot cluster around four passages — theft from the convert, the Nazirite vow, the priestly blessing, and the princes' offerings.
Across thirty years she sharpened the same questions in different keys.
Strikingly, she avoided Sotah almost entirely. Not one sheet headlined the trial of the suspected adulteress.

text.en: When a person commits any wrong against another, the Torah commands: confess, restore the principal, add one-fifth, bring a ram.
On the surface: a passage about restitution.
But the Torah calls a sin between people a trespass against the Lord.
And it builds the whole passage around the strangest case: a creditor with no kin.
Nechama wrote five gilyonot on these six verses. Below: three of her angles, across twenty-four years.

Nine years later — the headline shifts. The midrash of the deer that left the wilderness, and R. Nathan reading the verse forward.
The late return. An entire gilayon on a single word: ḥomesh. What it is, when it applies, how it's calculated.

text.en: Gilayon תש״ד / 1944. Nechama's first treatment of this passage.
She organizes seven cruxes. We follow three.
First: a strange asymmetry in the law of restitution.

steps.ref: Mishneh Torah, Robbery and Lost Property 7:1, 7:8

text.he: הלכה א: כל מי שנתחייב ממון לחברו הישראלי וכפר בו ונשבע על שקר, הרי זה חייב להחזיר לו הקרן שכפר בו והוספת חומש וחייב בקרבן… הלכה ח: אין הנשבע על כפירת ממון משלם חומש עד שיודה מעצמו, אבל אם באו עדים והוא עומד בכפירתו משלם הקרן בלבד על פי עדים ואינו משלם החומש.
text.en: Halakhah 1: Anyone who owed money to a fellow Israelite, denied it, and swore falsely — he must return the principal he denied, add a fifth, and bring an offering… Halakhah 8: The one who swears falsely about a denial of money does not pay the fifth until he confesses on his own; if witnesses came and he remained in his denial, he pays the principal alone on the testimony of witnesses, and does not pay the fifth.

annotation.en: Witnesses get you the principal. The fifth is triggered only by voluntary confession. The Torah builds the law so that honesty costs more than getting caught.

text.en: What is the inner logic? Why does confessing voluntarily cost the wrongdoer more than being convicted in court?
Second: why is a sin against another person called a trespass against the Lord?

text.he: ר' עקיבא אומר: מה תלמוד לומר "למעול מעל בה'"? לפי שהמלווה והלווה והנושא והנותן אינו מלווה ואינו לווה ואינו נושא ונותן אלא בשטר ובעדים, לפיכך בזמן שהוא מכחיש, מכחיש בעדים ובשטר. אבל המפקיד אצל חברו, אינו רוצה שתדע בו נשמה אלא שלישי שביניהם — בזמן שהוא מכחיש, מכחיש בשלישי שביניהם.
text.en: R. Akiva said: Why does the verse say 'to commit a trespass against the Lord'? Because lenders, borrowers, buyers and sellers transact only with a contract and witnesses — so when one of them denies, he denies in the face of witnesses and a contract. But one who entrusts a deposit to his fellow does not want any third party to know — only the One between them. When he denies, he denies the One between them.

annotation.en: R. Akiva resolves the verse's puzzle: in the open marketplace there is no false oath against God — the lying targets witnesses. But in the private deposit, where only God is the witness, denying becomes a denial of God.

text.en: What difficulty in the verse is R. Akiva resolving — and what does his answer say about the role of secrecy in sin?
Third: and whom is the passage really about?

text.he: ד"ה ואם אין לאיש גואל: שמת התובע שהשביעו ואין לו יורשים. ואמרו רבותינו: וכי יש לך אדם בישראל שאין לו גואלים, או בן או בת או אח או שאר בשר הקרוב ממשפחת אביו למעלה עד יעקב? אלא, זה הגר שמת ואין לו יורשים.
text.en: "If the man has no kin" — the claimant who put him under oath has died and left no heirs. Our Rabbis asked: Is there any Israelite who has no kinsman whatsoever — without a son, a brother, or any relative going back to Jacob? But this refers to the convert who died, who has no heirs.

annotation.en: The convert who left a pagan family — under Jewish law his birth kin are not recognized. He is the only one in Israel who can truly stand alone. The Torah writes the law of theft from his vantage point.

text.en: Read this way, the heirless convert is not an edge case. He is the case.
Why does the Torah locate the general law of restitution from the vantage point of the most vulnerable creditor — one who, by definition, can no longer collect?

text.en: Gilayon תשי״ג / 1953. Nine years on, the headline of her sheet has changed.
She titles this sheet אַהֲבַת הַגֵּר — Love of the Convert. And she opens not with the verse but with a midrash.

text.he: "איש או אשה" — הדא הוא דכתיב (תהלים קמ"ו) "ה' אוהב צדיקים". כך אמר הקב"ה (משלי ח') "אני אוהבי אהב"… ולמה הקב"ה אוהב צדיקים? שאינן בנחלה ואינן במשפחה. אתה מוצא הכוהנים — בית אב, הלויים — בית אב… אלא הגרים אינן בנחלה ואינן במשפחה — לפיכך הקב"ה אוהבם, שנאמר "ואוהב גר".
text.en: 'A man or a woman' — this is what is written (Psalms 146): 'The Lord loves the righteous.' So said the Holy One (Proverbs 8): 'I love those who love Me'… Why does the Holy One love the righteous? Because they are without inheritance and without lineage. The priests have a household, the Levites have a household… But the converts have no inheritance and no lineage — therefore the Holy One loves them, as it says, 'and He loves the convert.'

annotation.en: The midrash never says the word 'convert' — but Nechama hears it everywhere. The convert and the priest stand on the same ground: no inheritance, no family to fall back on. The deer that leaves the wide wilderness for the courtyard.

text.en: How do we know this passage is about robbing the convert, when the convert is never mentioned by name? And what is the midrash teaching by choosing a deer who leaves the wilderness?
Then she turns to the grammar of confession.

text.he: ד"ה והתודו: איזה מהם שיהיה, איש או אשה.
text.en: "They shall confess" — whichever of them it might be, man or woman.

annotation.en: Ibn Ezra catches a small grammatical fact: the plural verb 'they shall confess' has a singular subject — 'a man or a woman.' Why the plural? He answers minimally: it means whichever it is.

text.en: Why does the Torah use the reflexive form וְהִתְוַדּוּ — 'confess to themselves' — rather than the simpler וְהוֹדוּ, 'they shall acknowledge,' as in Proverbs?
And finally, a Talmudic reading that takes the last words of the verse with a startling literalness.

text.he: ר' נתן אומר: מניין לנושה בחברו מנה וחברו בחברו — מניין שמוציאין מזה ונותנים לזה? תלמוד לומר: "וְנָתַן לַאֲשֶׁר אָשַׁם לוֹ".
text.en: R. Nathan said: From where do we know that if A is owed by B, and B is owed by C, the court can collect from C and give to A? Scripture says: 'And he shall give it to the one to whom he is guilty.'

annotation.en: R. Nathan reads the 'him' of 'to whom he is guilty' as transitive — chaining forward through the chain of debts. The shevu'a-de-Rabbi-Natan, the right of indirect collection, is built from this single phrase.

text.en: Is the אָשָׁם of our verse the same as the וְאָשְׁמָה הַנֶּפֶשׁ two verses above — or has the Talmud given it a new sense entirely?

text.en: Gilayon תשכ״ח / 1968. Twenty-four years after her first sheet, Nechama returns once more.
And now she spends seven sections on a single word: חוֹמֶשׁ. The fifth.
First: Rashi notices that this whole law was already given in Leviticus 5. Why repeat it here?

text.he: ד"ה למעול מעל: הרי חזר וכתב כאן פרשת גוזל ונשבע על שקר, היא האמורה בפרשת ויקרא… ונשנית כאן בשביל שני דברים שנתחדשו בה: האחד, שכתוב "והתודו" — לומר שאינו חייב חומש ואשם על פי עדים עד שיודה בדבר. והשני, על גזל הגר, שהוא ניתן לכוהנים.
text.en: Scripture repeats here the passage of one who robs and swears falsely — it is the same passage stated in Leviticus 5. It is repeated here for two new points: first, that 'they shall confess' is written — to teach that one is not liable for the fifth and the guilt-offering on the testimony of witnesses, only when he confesses himself. Second, the law of robbing the convert — that the payment goes to the priests.

annotation.en: Rashi's economy: a whole repeated chapter, justified by exactly two new clauses. Everything else is summary. The chapter exists to make these two points.

text.en: Why does the Torah ask less of the convicted thief than of the one who confesses on his own?
Second: she compares two laws side by side — the punishment of the thief who breaks in, and the robber who takes by force.

text.he: ולמה החמירה תורה על הגנב יותר מן הגזלן? לפי שהגזלן הִשְׁוָה כְּבוֹד עבד לכבוד קוֹנוֹ. שלא נתיירא מן הרואים אותו, ולא חשש שמא ישמעו, ועשה בפרהסיא. אבל הגנב גנב בסתר, נתיירא מן הרואים, וכאילו עשה עין של מטה שאינה רואה ואוזן שאינה שומעת — לכן הוצרכה התורה להחמיר עליו.
text.en: Why did the Torah deal more strictly with the thief than with the robber? Because the robber treated the honor of the servant equal to the honor of his Master — he did not fear those who saw him, did not worry that they might hear, and acted openly. But the thief stole in secret. He feared those who saw, as if he made the lower eye blind and the lower ear deaf — therefore the Torah had to deal more strictly with him.

annotation.en: The robber acts in broad daylight; he fears no one — God and man are alike in his contempt. The thief hides, which means he fears people more than God. The hiding is the deeper sin.

text.en: Why does open brazenness pay less than hidden cunning? What is Rambam saying about the kind of fear the Torah wants — and the kind it punishes?
And finally: the actual math of the fifth.

text.he: "וְיָסַף חֲמִשִׁתוֹ עָלָיו" — שיהא הוא וחומשו חמשה; דברי ר' יאשיה. (רש"י: היינו חומש מִלְּבָר, שהוא רביע הקרן.) ר' יונתן אומר: חומש בראש, שיוסיף עליו חומשו עצמו.
text.en: "He shall add its fifth to it" — meaning that it and its fifth shall be five [parts]; these are R. Yashia's words. (Rashi: that is, a fifth from outside, which is a quarter of the principal.) R. Yonatan said: a fifth above — that he shall add to it its own fifth.

annotation.en: Two readings of one word. R. Yashia: 'fifth' means principal + fifth = 5 parts, so the fifth is one-quarter of the principal. R. Yonatan: 'fifth' means literally one-fifth of the principal. The same Torah, two arithmetics.

text.en: Which calculation does the language of our verse most naturally support — and what hangs on the choice?

text.en: Someone steps out of the ordinary stream of life — for thirty days, or a year, or longer — and consecrates himself to the Lord.
No wine. No haircut. No contact with the dead.
Hair set apart for his God upon his head.
The Torah doesn't say whether this is praiseworthy or troubling. And the silence is what generated centuries of dispute.
Nechama wrote four gilyonot on the Nazirite. Below: three of them.

text.en: Gilayon תש״ב / 1942. Nechama's first gilayon — composed in the second year of her Sokhnut series.
She opens at the moment the Torah hardest to interpret: the Nazirite, having safely completed his term, must bring a sin-offering.
The verse explains: 'for that he sinned by reason of a soul.' But which soul — and what was the sin?

text.he: ד"ה מאשר חטא על הנפש: שלא נזהר מטומאת המת. ר' אלעזר הקפר אומר: שצִעֵר עצמו מן היין.
text.en: "For that he sinned by reason of a soul" — because he was not careful about defilement by a corpse. R. Elazar HaKappar says: because he afflicted himself by abstaining from wine.

annotation.en: Rashi gives the verse's plain reading first — the sin is the lapse, the encounter with death. Then he sets R. Elazar HaKappar's explosive alternative beside it: the sin is the Naziriteship itself. Two readings, one verse.

text.en: The stakes are enormous.
On the first reading, the Nazirite who never touched a corpse and finished his term cleanly owes no atonement at all.
On R. Elazar HaKappar's reading, every completed Nazirite is a sinner — the renunciation itself was the trespass.
If R. Elazar HaKappar is right, what is the Torah's view of one who renounces permitted pleasures 'for the Lord'? Praise — or warning?
And Rambam offers the synthesis Nechama will follow for the rest of her life.

text.he: שמא יאמר אדם: הואיל והקנאה והתאוה והכבוד וכיוצא בהן דרך רעה הן ומוציאין את האדם מן העולם, אפרוש מהן ביותר ואתרחק לצד האחרון, עד שלא יאכל בשר ולא ישתה יין ולא ישא אשה ולא ישב בדירה נאה ולא ילבש מלבוש נאה אלא השק והצמר הקשה וכיוצא בהן, כגון כומרי אדום. גם זה דרך רעה היא, ואסור לילך בה. המהלך בדרך זו נקרא חוטא… ולפיכך ציוו חכמים שלא ימנע אדם עצמו אלא מדברים שמנעתהו התורה בלבד.
text.en: Lest a person say: since envy and lust and honor and the like are evil ways that drive a person from the world, I will distance myself from them to the utmost — not eating meat, not drinking wine, not marrying, not living in a fine house, wearing only sackcloth and coarse wool, like the Christian monks. This too is an evil path, and one is forbidden to walk in it. One who walks in it is called a sinner… Therefore the Sages commanded: a person should deny himself only what the Torah has forbidden.

annotation.en: Rambam's golden mean. The Nazirite oversteps. Renunciation of the permitted is not piety — it is a sinner's path. The sin-offering at the end is the Torah's price tag on the excess.

text.en: Does Rambam's reading make every Nazirite a sinner — or does it leave room for the Nazirite who actually needed the discipline?

text.en: Gilayon תש״ו / 1946. Four years later, Nechama reframes.
She takes the same verse — 'for that he sinned by reason of a soul' — and now reads it through Ramban.
Ramban accepts the question in its sharpest form: why does the Torah call the Nazirite a sinner?
But he moves the moment of sin.
It is not the abstention. It is the ending.

text.he: ועל דרך הפשט, כי האיש הזה חוטא נפשו בִּמְלֹאת הַנְּזִירוּת. כי הוא עתה נָזוֹר מקדושתו ועבודת השם. וראוי היה לו שיזיר לעולם ויעמוד כל ימיו נזיר וקדוש לאלוהיו. והנה הוא צריך כפרה בשובו להיטמא בתאוות העולם.
text.en: According to the plain meaning: this person sins against his soul at the completion of his Naziriteship — for he is now departing from his sanctity and the service of God. He should have remained a Nazirite forever, abiding all his days holy unto his God. He requires atonement upon returning to be defiled by the desires of the world.

annotation.en: Ramban inverts Rambam. The Nazirite period was the correction. Re-entering ordinary life — with its wine and weddings and grief — is the lapse. The sin-offering is paid on the way back down.

text.en: Ramban anchors this in Amos.

text.he: וָאָקִים מִבְּנֵיכֶם לִנְבִיאִים וּמִבַּחוּרֵיכֶם לִנְזִרִים. הַאַף אֵין זֹאת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל — נְאֻם ה'.
text.en: I raised up some of your sons for prophets, and some of your young men for Nazirites. Is this not so, O people of Israel? — declares the Lord.

annotation.en: Prophet and Nazirite stand in the same syntax. Both are a calling. Ending a Nazirite vow is, on this reading, like resigning prophecy.

text.en: If returning to ordinary life requires atonement, what does the Torah think ordinary life is?
Is Ramban's inversion of Rambam a dispute about the Nazirite — or about Judaism itself?

text.en: Gilayon תש״ל / 1970. Twenty-eight years after her first Nazir sheet — and her last.
By 1970 she no longer organizes the page as a series of multi-source cruxes. It is an essay. She is, after all, almost seventy.
She returns to the figure of the Nazirite as the person who reaches outside the average path.
She leans on a quieter medieval voice — Hizkuni, the thirteenth-century French Tosafist — to carry the question forward.

text.he: כי יפליא — לשון הפלאה ופרישות. דבר הפלא בעיני הבריות הוא, כי לא ירצה בתענוגי העולם הזה.
text.en: 'Explicitly utters' — the word evokes hafla'ah, separation. It is a wondrous thing in people's eyes, for the Nazirite does not desire the pleasures of this world.

annotation.en: The Nazirite is a wonder. Not a saint, not a sinner — but a person who, in the eyes of the neighbors, has done something inexplicable. Hizkuni reads יפליא as the cousin of פלא — a miracle of self-shaping.

text.en: Nechama, late in her life: 'The Nazirite is the human capacity to step out of the usual.'
The earlier sheets had asked: is this praised or punished? By 1970 her question has shifted.
She asks instead: what does it cost to be a wonder — to oneself, to one's neighbors, to one's God?
Is religious life made of the average — kept up by everyone — or of the wondrous, sustained by the few who can bear it?

text.en: Three lines, growing from three Hebrew words to five to seven.
Found inscribed on silver amulets from the First Temple period — older than almost any other text recited in Jewish liturgy.
And ending with the most surprising line of all.
If only God can really bless — what are the priests actually doing?

If only God can make a person flourish — if a human saying 'may you flourish' does not, in itself, make anyone flourish — what is the priest actually doing?

text.he: ד"ה ואני אברכם: לישראל. ואסכים עם הכוהנים. דבר אחר: ואני אברכם — לכוהנים.
text.en: "And I will bless them" — i.e., the Israelites: I will give My assent to the priests' blessing. Another interpretation: 'and I will bless them' — meaning the priests.

annotation.en: Rashi chooses an extraordinary word for what God does: הַסְכָּמָה — 'I give My consent.' The priest's blessing is not the blessing. It is the human gesture toward which God then bends.

text.en: She glosses Rashi through a parable from R. Hayim Yosef Polak.

text.he: השוה ברכת ה' לגשם היורד על הארץ. הגשם הוא מן השמים — וכך הברכה. אבל הקרקע היא שמכריעה מה יהיה ממנו. הכוהן אינו עושה את הגשם, אלא מכין את הקרקע לקבלה.
text.en: Compare the Lord's blessing to rain falling on the earth. The rain comes from heaven — and so does the blessing. But the soil decides what becomes of it. The priest does not make the rain; he prepares the soil to receive it.

annotation.en: The priest's role is not to make rain. It is to make Israel ready for rain. The blessing is what God will do. The standing-still-in-front-of-the-priest is what we contribute.

text.en: Read this way, the command "Thus shall you bless" is not addressed to the recipient's flourishing.
It is addressed to the recipient's receptivity.
If the priest's blessing is preparation, not power — what other commanded gestures in Jewish life make sense the same way?

text.en: Gilayon תשט״ו / 1955. Nechama's densest treatment of any single passage in Nasso.
Five sections, one for each phrase. Three verses, growing — three words, five, seven.
The first: bless and keep. Three words — a basic request. Flourishing and protection.
The second: shining face and grace. No longer only material gifts — but a gaze. Five words.
The third: lifting His face, and peace. Maximum intimacy. Seven words. And peace at the end.

text.he: וְיָשֵׂם לְךָ שָׁלוֹם — שלום בביתך. דבר אחר: שלא יהיה דבר רע ביוצא ובא.
text.en: "And grant you peace" — peace in your house. Another interpretation: that nothing bad shall come out from you or in to you.

annotation.en: Rashi domesticates the climax. The peace is the homestead — the absence of trouble entering or leaving the door. The biggest gift is the smallest scene.

text.en: And Nechama asks the question Rashi doesn't quite answer.
Why does the blessing end in peace? Why not in blessing itself? Why not in illumination?
Perhaps because, as the Mishnah teaches: the Holy One found no vessel that holds blessing for Israel except peace.

text.en: Gilayon תשכ״ב / 1962. Nechama steps back.
She titles this gilayon מבנה הפרשה וברכת כהנים — The Structure of the Parsha and the Priestly Blessing.
The question: why is the priestly blessing here?
Before it: the Sotah, the trial of the suspected adulteress. After it: the Nazirite. And then: the Princes' offerings.
Why does the blessing sit in the middle of all this?

steps.ref: R. Samson Raphael Hirsch on Numbers 6:22

text.he: ברכת הכוהנים באה אחרי שתי פרשות העוסקות בנפילות אפשריות — סוטה ונזיר. שתיהן עוסקות בכישלון אנושי או בתגובה לכישלון אנושי. ולכן בא צו לכוהנים: כך תברכו את ישראל. הברכה אינה תוצאה של שלמות; היא קודמת לה.
text.en: The priestly blessing comes after two passages dealing with possible falls — Sotah and Nazir. Both deal with human failure or the reaction to human failure. And so the command comes to the priests: thus shall you bless Israel. The blessing is not the product of perfection. It precedes it.

annotation.en: Hirsch reads the editorial seam. Israel has been shown the trial of mistrust (Sotah) and the path of withdrawal (Nazir). And then — before the celebration of the princes' offerings — God commands a blessing. The blessing is not the reward at the end. It is the floor on which everything else stands.

text.en: Read this way, the position of the blessing IS the lesson.
Israel is given a blessing before the wedding (the princes' gifts), and after the trial (Sotah and Nazir).
If the priestly blessing is placed after failure and before celebration, what is the Torah teaching about when a community most needs to hear that God's face is turned toward it?

primaryText.he: וַיְהִי בְּיוֹם כַּלּוֹת מֹשֶׁה לְהָקִים אֶת הַמִּשְׁכָּן וַיִּמְשַׁח אֹתוֹ וַיְקַדֵּשׁ אֹתוֹ וְאֶת כׇּל כֵּלָיו וְאֶת הַמִּזְבֵּחַ וְאֶת כׇּל כֵּלָיו וַיִּמְשָׁחֵם וַיְקַדֵּשׁ אֹתָם וַיַּקְרִיבוּ נְשִׂיאֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל רָאשֵׁי בֵּית אֲבֹתָם הֵם נְשִׂיאֵי הַמַּטֹּת הֵם הָעֹמְדִים עַל הַפְּקֻדִים וַיָּבִיאוּ אֶת קׇרְבָּנָם לִפְנֵי יְהֹוָה שֵׁשׁ עֶגְלֹת צָב וּשְׁנֵי עָשָׂר בָּקָר עֲגָלָה עַל שְׁנֵי הַנְּשִׂאִים וְשׁוֹר לְאֶחָד וַיַּקְרִיבוּ אוֹתָם לִפְנֵי הַמִּשְׁכָּן
primaryText.en: On the day that Moses finished setting up the Mishkan, he anointed and consecrated it and all its furnishings, as well as the altar and its utensils. When he had anointed and consecrated them, the princes of Israel, the heads of ancestral houses, namely, the princes of the tribes, those who were in charge of enrollment, drew near and brought their offering before the Lord: six draught carts and twelve oxen, a cart for every two princes and an ox for each one. They brought them before the Mishkan.

text.en: After the laws comes the longest narrative passage in the Torah by sheer repetition.
Twelve princes. Twelve days. Twelve identical offerings, written out twelve times.
The same silver dish, the same bull, the same goat — listed again, and again, and again.
The Torah does not normally waste words. Brevity is its house style.
Nechama wrote seven gilyonot circling one question.
What is the repetition doing?

text.en: Gilayon תשי״ז / 1957. Nechama's first sheet on the Princes' offerings.
She organizes four sections. The first asks why each prince's offering is described separately at all.

text.he: ולמה פירט כל קרבן וקרבן בפני עצמו, אף על פי שהיו שווים? מפני שהיו כל אחד ואחד חביב לפניו כאילו הקריב לבדו.
text.en: Why did Scripture detail each offering on its own, even though they were identical? Because each one of them was beloved before Him as if he alone had offered.

annotation.en: The midrash gives the simplest answer. The Torah refuses to compress. Each prince's day is its own day. The redundancy is not waste — it is dignity, twelvefold.

text.en: Compare what the Torah doesn't repeat. Six days of creation: summed up. Forty years in the wilderness: summed up.
But for twelve identical offerings, the same recipe appears in full twelve times.
Then she asks who these princes were.

text.he: ד"ה הם העומדים על הפקודים: שעמדו עליהם בעת המנין, שנאמר "ואִתְּכֶם יהיו איש איש למטה".
text.en: "Those who were in charge of the enrollment" — they were the ones who stood over the people at the census, as Scripture says: 'and with you shall be a man of each tribe.'

annotation.en: Rashi connects this verse to the census back in chapter 1. The princes are not strangers walking up to the altar. They are the same twelve men who counted Israel. The Torah is closing a loop.

text.en: Whose attention is the Torah protecting by refusing to abbreviate? The princes' — or Israel's?

text.en: Gilayon תש״כ / 1960. Three years on, Nechama returns — and now she writes eleven sections.
The headline of section א: יִזְכּוֹר הַכָּתוּב לְכָל אֶחָד בִּשְׁמוֹ — 'Scripture remembers each by name.'

text.he: כי השלמות האנושית אינה בכלל המין בלבד, ככל שאר הנמצאות ההוות ונפסדות, אלא בפרט — באיש איש בפני עצמו. ועל זה אמר הכתוב 'יזכור הכתוב לכל אחד בשמו', שכן זוהי מעלת האדם: שכל אחד הוא עולם מלא.
text.en: Human perfection does not lie in the species alone, as it does in other beings that come into existence and pass away — it lies in the particular, in each individual on his own. Therefore Scripture remembers each one by name: for this is the human dignity — that each one is a world entire.

annotation.en: R. Yitzhak Arama: humans, unlike other creatures, exist as individuals, not just as species. The Torah's twelvefold repetition is a doctrine of personhood. To merge them would be to treat them like cattle. To repeat them is to acknowledge that each one is a world.

text.en: But then Nechama turns to the other side of the question.
If each prince is honored by name, what does the Torah mean by giving them all the same offering?

text.he: אף שהיו שווים בקרבן, היו חלוקים בכוונה ובמחשבה. וכל אחד כיוון לסוד שבטו, לתפקיד שבטו בעולם.
text.en: Although they were equal in their offering, they differed in their intention and inner thought. Each one directed himself toward the secret of his tribe, toward the role of his tribe in the world.

annotation.en: Malbim: the gift is identical, the giver is not. Twelve men brought twelve different prayers in one cattle-and-silver currency. The repetition is a portrait gallery in plain frames.

text.en: Section ד of the 1960 sheet is titled שֶׁלֹּא יָגִיס דַּעְתּוֹ — 'so he should not become arrogant.'
The princes are great, but they are not first. Moses is first; the priests are first; the Mishkan is first.
Their offerings come only after the structure is built and the priests are anointed.
How does the Torah honor each prince by name without letting any one of them mistake honor for primacy?

text.en: Gilayon תשכ״ו / 1966. Nechama opens with the answer she has been circling for nine years.
It comes from a fourteenth-century Provençal philosopher named R. Yosef Ibn Kaspi.
He wrote a slim book called Tirat Kesef. In it, he says something Nechama will quote for the rest of her life.

text.he: אריכות לשון נמצא ברוב בספר תורתנו, במה שהוא נתלה בעניין הכלל. ומתחלף זה עם דרך הפילוסופים, שיכתבו לחכמים ולמלומדים, אשר יסבלו ההפשטה ולא יצטרכו לחזרה. אבל התורה דיברה ללשון בני אדם, אל ההמון הרחב — והדבר אשר צריך שיודע צריך שייאמר פעם ופעמים, עד שיובן.
text.en: Lengthiness of expression is found often in the Book of our Torah, especially in matters concerning the entire people. This differs from the way of the philosophers, who write for the wise and learned — those who can bear abstraction and do not require repetition. But the Torah speaks in human language, to the broad multitude — and what must be known must be said once and again, until it is grasped.

annotation.en: Ibn Kaspi's hinge. A philosopher writes for readers who can hold an abstraction. The Torah writes for everyone — and most people only wake to a truth when it is repeated. The redundancy is not a flaw. It is what the writing is for.

text.en: Nechama then presses a second reading, alongside Ibn Kaspi's.
To list each prince's gift separately — even when the gift is identical — is to refuse to compress them into a list.
Each prince's day is its own day.
The repetition is not pedagogical inefficiency. It is the Torah declining to make twelve people into one footnote.
Are Ibn Kaspi and the midrashic 'dignity' reading two readings — or one reading from two sides? Pedagogy of the people, dignity of the person?

title.en: 1969 · Like a Bride to the Canopy

primaryText.he: וַיְהִי בְּיוֹם כַּלּוֹת מֹשֶׁה לְהָקִים אֶת הַמִּשְׁכָּן וַיִּמְשַׁח אֹתוֹ וַיְקַדֵּשׁ אֹתוֹ וְאֶת כׇּל כֵּלָיו וְאֶת הַמִּזְבֵּחַ וְאֶת כׇּל כֵּלָיו וַיִּמְשָׁחֵם וַיְקַדֵּשׁ אֹתָם וַיַּקְרִיבוּ נְשִׂיאֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל רָאשֵׁי בֵּית אֲבֹתָם הֵם נְשִׂיאֵי הַמַּטֹּת הֵם הָעֹמְדִים עַל הַפְּקֻדִים וַיָּבִיאוּ אֶת קׇרְבָּנָם לִפְנֵי יְהֹוָה שֵׁשׁ עֶגְלֹת צָב וּשְׁנֵי עָשָׂר בָּקָר עֲגָלָה עַל שְׁנֵי הַנְּשִׂאִים וְשׁוֹר לְאֶחָד וַיַּקְרִיבוּ אוֹתָם לִפְנֵי הַמִּשְׁכָּן
primaryText.en: On the day that Moses finished setting up the Mishkan, he anointed and consecrated it and all its furnishings, as well as the altar and its utensils. When he had anointed and consecrated them, the princes of Israel, the heads of ancestral houses, namely, the princes of the tribes, those who were in charge of enrollment, drew near and brought their offering before the Lord: six draught carts and twelve oxen, a cart for every two princes and an ox for each one. They brought them before the Mishkan.

text.en: Gilayon תשכ״ט / 1969. Nechama's final sheet on Parshat Nasso.
She returns to Numbers 7:1 — 'On the day Moses finished setting up the Mishkan.'
And she lingers, this final time, on a defective spelling: כַּלּוֹת is written without the second waw — read as כַּלַּת, 'bride.'

text.he: ד"ה ביום כלות משה: כלת כתיב. יום הקמת המשכן היו ישראל ככלה הנכנסת לחופה.
text.en: "On the day Moses finished" — kallat is written defective [as if reading 'bride']. On the day the Mishkan was erected, Israel was like a bride entering the wedding canopy.

annotation.en: Rashi turns a verse about construction into a wedding scene. The Mishkan is the canopy. Israel is the bride. The princes' offerings that follow — twelve days of gifts — are the wedding gifts.

text.en: Read this way, all the strange features of the chapter fall into place.
The elaborate repetition? Gift-giving at a wedding is ceremonial. Each present is named. Each giver is honored. Each moment is its own.
The careful order? At a wedding, the procession matters.
And the gilayon's final section returns to Ibn Kaspi — the same passage she had quoted in 1966 — to ask why the Torah's longest scene of repetition is also the Torah's most intimate.
If chapter 7 is a wedding, what changed on that day for Israel — and what changed for God?
Her 1969 sheet is signed off with the same hand that wrote the first in 1942.
Twenty-seven years. Twenty-eight gilyonot. One bride. Walk back up; choose again.
